A putsch is a sudden, forceful attempt by a small group of people to seize control of a government — overnight if possible — by using violence, the threat of violence, or military force, rather than through elections, laws, or any legitimate political process.

Think of it this way: in a democracy, if you want power, you campaign and win an election. In a putsch, you skip all of that and simply grab power — with guns, troops, or brute intimidation.

Here are the defining features of a putsch, all of which must be present for it to truly qualify as one:

1. It is sudden.
A putsch doesn't build slowly over years like a political movement. It strikes fast — typically in hours or days. The whole point is to catch the existing government off guard, before it can react or defend itself.

2. It is carried out by a small, organised group.
A putsch is not a popular mass uprising where millions of ordinary people take to the streets. It is orchestrated by a tight, specific group — most commonly military officers, political extremists, or a faction within the government itself. The general public is largely a bystander, not a participant.

3. It is violent, or at least backed by the threat of violence.
A putsch always involves force or the credible threat of it. Soldiers seizing buildings, armed groups taking over radio and TV stations, troops surrounding the presidential palace — these are the tools of a putsch. Without force (or the threatening shadow of it), it's just a political manoeuvre, not a putsch.

4. Its goal is to seize state power.
The group carrying out the putsch wants to take control of the government itself — not just protest it, not just influence it, but replace it. They want to sit in the seat of power.

5. It is illegal and unconstitutional.
By definition, a putsch bypasses every legal and democratic mechanism that exists. It is a crime against the state, even if the people committing it believe they are saving the nation.

Because "putsch" sits in a neighbourhood of similar-sounding political words, it helps to clearly separate them.

  • Coup d'état: This is the closest relative — so close that the two terms are often used interchangeably, and correctly so. "Coup" is the French term; "putsch" is the German term. Both describe the same basic act. However, in practice, "putsch" is slightly more likely to be used when the attempt fails or when it is carried out by a fringe/extremist group. "Coup" is the more neutral, general, and internationally common term. If a coup succeeds, you rarely hear it called a putsch afterwards. If it fails spectacularly, "putsch" tends to stick.
  • Revolution: A revolution is a large-scale, popular upheaval that fundamentally transforms a society — its government, its social order, its values. Revolutions are driven by masses of people and often unfold over months or years. A putsch involves a small group, happens fast, and is only about grabbing governmental power — it doesn't necessarily change anything about society itself.
  • Insurrection / Rebellion: These are armed uprisings against an authority, but they don't necessarily aim to replace the government with the rebels themselves at the helm. A putsch has a very specific, targeted goal: take over the state.
  • Assassination: Killing a leader is not a putsch. A putsch means seizing the governmental machinery — the institutions, the ministries, the military chain of command. Simply removing one person, without taking control of the system, is not a putsch.
Does a Putsch Have to Succeed?

No — and this is important.

The word "putsch" is used for both successful and failed attempts, but historically it is most famously associated with failed attempts. In fact, a failed putsch is still called a putsch. Success is not part of the definition. If it succeeds and holds, it typically gets relabelled over time — as a "coup," a "revolution," or simply "a change of government." The word "putsch" tends to linger most strongly around the dramatic failures.

The Beer Hall Putsch (Germany, 1923) — The most textbook example of the word. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party, a fringe extremist group at the time, attempted to overthrow the Weimar Republic government of Germany. They burst into a beer hall in Munich where government officials were gathered, took them hostage at gunpoint, and tried to ignite a national uprising. The following day, when they marched through the streets, police opened fire. The putsch collapsed within hours. Sixteen Nazis and four police officers died. Hitler was arrested, tried, and imprisoned. The attempt was a total failure — yet it made Hitler nationally famous and is one of the most studied putsche in history.

The Kapp Putsch (Germany, 1920) — Just three years earlier, a right-wing military officer named Wolfgang Kapp and a brigade of soldiers marched on Berlin and briefly seized the capital, forcing the legitimate government to flee. However, when workers across the country responded with a massive general strike — shutting down electricity, transport, and industry — the putsch collapsed within four days because the conspirators couldn't actually run the country.

The Soviet Coup Attempt (USSR, 1991) — Communist hardliners, alarmed that Mikhail Gorbachev was loosening the Soviet system, placed him under house arrest and announced they had taken control of the government. But the public resisted, soldiers refused to fire on civilians, and within three days the putsch had fallen apart. Its failure directly accelerated the collapse of the Soviet Union itself.
The Emotional and Political Weight of the Word

"Putsch" is not a neutral, dry technical term. When someone uses it, they are making a clear moral and political judgement: this was illegitimate. It wasn't a rightful transfer of power — it was a power grab. The word carries a tone of condemnation. Governments that survive putsche use the word proudly to delegitimise the attackers. Historians use it to mark these events as fundamentally anti-democratic, regardless of the ideology of the group that attempted them.

A putsch is a fast, forceful, illegal seizure of government power by a small organised group — done through violence or military force, not through democratic or legal means. It is most strongly associated with failure, and the word itself carries a tone of political illegitimacy and condemnation.
